newsitem.title: UK: Sagging gold fixes below key $350 level.
newsitem.headline: Sagging gold fixes below key $350 level.

text.p: Fresh selling pushed gold prices back below the key $350 level in early European trading on Thursday in a bullion market that seemed ready to extend its recent slide.
Dealers said little was preventing gold from re-testing last week's low of $346 an ounce -- the lowest gold has been since September 1993.
Bullion was fixed at $349.30 an ounce, compared to $351.10 on Wednesday afternoon and a London close of $350.80/$351.30.
Earlier this week prices had moved sharply higher, hitting a high above $357, only to tumble in an equally steep correction. Dealers reported a low bid of $349.05 in early trading.
Fresh institutional selling had come into the bearish, disappointed market to push gold lower in early trading, mimicking a similar move on Wednesday morning, dealers said.
"The timing was the same as yesterday suggesting a selling programme. This was quality selling," a dealer said.
Prices subsequently bounced slightly ahead of the fixing, and dealers reported two-way business just above $349. But another bout of selling would easily push prices lower.
"The next port of call may be $348," one said.
"But every time it tests this level, support is eaten away. Sellers are going to outnumber buyers and when it goes through it's going to head to $342."
By contrast silver was unchanged from Wednesday's close at $4.91/$4.92. Prices had slipped slightly with gold in early trading but bounced up from a low of $4.88 an ounce.
Platinum, however, was closely following gold and was indicated $2.00 lower at $352.75/$353.75.
It was expected to find some support around $352, and a dip to $350 would likely attract consumer buying, he said.
"Platinum is just following gold which looks pretty awful today. There are just bits and pieces of business, it's just being marked down," a dealer said.
On Wednesday, however Japanese selling had come in due to weakness in the yen, he added.

A platinum industry source said in Tokyo that platinum demand from the Japanese jewellery industry in 1996 maintained the previous year's record high of 46 tonnes. But that figure may slip this year, he added.
Demand from the jewellery sector makes up about 70 percent of platinum demand in major consumer Japan.
Palladium, which has been trending higher since early December in contrast to the other precious metals, was up $0.25 at $121.00/$122.00.
